plans.title: Keep the current rotation
plans.review: Check with your local extension office or conservation district before changing practice.
plans.rationale: What the field has been doing: lentils in 3 of 7 years, winter wheat in 3 of 7 years, spring wheat in 1 of 7 years.
plans.evidence: Crops: USDA Cropland Data Layer, 2019 to 2025. Bare weeks: NASA HLS greenness below 0.25 NDVI. Heavy-rain weeks: NASA POWER.
plans.benefits: No new cost and nothing to learn.
plans.gaps: About 3 weeks a year were hidden by cloud or snow. About 1 week a year are counted as likely bare across cloudy gaps, not seen.
plans.risks: Crop residue, tillage and slope are not measured. A field with good residue cover is better protected than its bare-week count suggests.
plans.reason: bare about 19 weeks a year (17 seen, 1 likely), 1 of them during heavy rain

plans.title: Add a cover crop
plans.review: Check with your local extension office or conservation district before changing practice.
plans.rationale: Plant a cover crop after harvest so the soil is not left open. We fill each bare stretch from 3 weeks after it starts, and leave alone the months winter wheat is in the ground.
plans.evidence: Crops: USDA Cropland Data Layer, 2019 to 2025. Bare weeks: NASA HLS greenness below 0.25 NDVI. Heavy-rain weeks: NASA POWER. The cover is applied to this field's own bare weeks.
plans.benefits: About 11 fewer bare weeks a year, 1 of them in heavy rain.
plans.gaps: This is a best case. We do not model whether a cover crop would come up in a dry late summer, or how much ground it would really cover.
plans.risks: Cover crops use soil water. WSU trials saw winter wheat yield about 20% less after forage cover crops in a dry spring and no difference in a wet one, and a review of temperate drylands found an average 11% drop.

water.note: Uses soil water the next crop may need.

income.note: Seed, planting and termination costs, with no immediate cash return.

plans.reason: bare about 8 weeks a year, almost none during heavy rain

plans.title: Change the rotation
plans.review: Check with your local extension office or conservation district before changing practice.
plans.rationale: Swap one lentils year (2025) for chick peas, a crop that fixes its own nitrogen, to break up a repeated crop.
plans.evidence: Crops: USDA Cropland Data Layer, 2019 to 2025. Bare weeks: NASA HLS greenness below 0.25 NDVI. Heavy-rain weeks: NASA POWER. The chick peas year uses the typical weekly pattern of 3631 chick peas field-years measured in this study area.
plans.benefits: More crop variety, which lifts the grade. WSU reports wheat after peas or lentils can yield 10 to 20% more than in a wheat-fallow rotation, and pulses help with grass weeds and disease.
plans.gaps: The swapped year is a typical pattern, not a forecast for this field. Effects on the following crop are not modelled.
plans.risks: Markets, equipment and disease history for the new crop are not in our data.

water.note: WSU ranks chick peas as using more water than lentils.

income.note: Depends on prices and yields, which are not in our data.

plans.reason: bare about 21 weeks a year (15 seen, 6 likely), 1 of them during heavy rain

soil.name: Palouse-Thatuna silt loams, 7 to 25 percent slopes
